intro: A mother lights a lamp before an image of Krishna. A monk in a saffron robe holds out his bowl at dawn. Volunteers at a gurdwara serve a free meal to anyone who walks in. A family in Japan bows at a shrine gate, then lights incense at a Buddhist temple down the hill. Each of these scenes belongs to a tradition that began in South or East Asia.

This unit explores seven of those traditions: Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism, Confucianism, Daoism and Shinto. You will read from their sacred texts, such as the Bhagavad Gita, the Dhammapada, the Analects and the Daodejing. You will see how they answer big questions about suffering, duty, nature and how to treat others. You will also see the variety inside each tradition.

Many of these traditions have deep roots in Chicago, from the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions to the temples and gurdwaras of today. By the end of the unit, you will be able to explain key terms in each tradition's own words, attribute each belief to its tradition and compare them fairly without ranking them.
bigQuestion: How do the traditions of South and East Asia teach people to find freedom, harmony and a good life?

timeline.t: Oldest hymns of the Rig Veda are composed and passed on by memory
The earliest Upanishads begin to be composed
Mahavira, Confucius and the Buddha teach, by traditional dating
Ashoka conquers Kalinga, then carves his regret in edicts
Buddhism reaches China along the Silk Road
China's civil-service exams on the Confucian classics begin
The Kojiki records Japan's ancient stories of the kami
Guru Nanak, first Guru of the Sikhs, is born in the Punjab
Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa
Hindu and Buddhist teachers speak at Chicago's World's Parliament of Religions
B. R. Ambedkar and many followers become Buddhists

words.d: in Hinduism, duty or the right way to live; in Buddhism, the Buddha's teaching
the teaching that actions bring results back to the one who acts
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth
in Hindu teaching, release from the cycle of rebirth
in Hindu thought, the one ultimate reality behind all things
in Buddhism, the end of craving and suffering and freedom from rebirth
the Buddha's teaching on suffering, its cause, its end and the path
the free shared meal served at every Sikh gurdwara
non-harm; the principle of not hurting any living being
in Confucian teaching, humaneness or goodness toward others
in Daoism, effortless action in harmony with nature
in Shinto, sacred powers or spirits in nature, ancestors and places

test.q: Which texts are the oldest Hindu scriptures?
test.why: The Vedas are the oldest Hindu scriptures.

test.q: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna teaches Arjuna to do what?
choices: do his duty without clinging to results
test.why: Gita 2.47 teaches action without attachment to its fruits.

test.q: Which word names release from the cycle of rebirth in Hindu teaching?
test.why: Moksha is release; samsara is the cycle itself.

test.q: What do Buddhists say is the cause of suffering?
test.why: The Second Noble Truth names craving as the cause.

test.q: Why is Ashoka important to Buddhist history?
choices: he supported the Buddha's teaching and helped it spread
he was the tenth Sikh Guru
test.why: After Kalinga, Ashoka supported Buddhism and, by tradition, sent teachers abroad.

test.q: Which Buddhist branch uses Pali scriptures and is common in Thailand?
test.why: Theravada uses the Pali scriptures and is common in Southeast Asia.

test.q: Hindus and Buddhists differ on which idea?
choices: whether there is a permanent self
test.why: Many Hindus speak of Atman; the Buddha taught no permanent self.

test.q: Which Sikh teaching does the langar show?
test.why: Everyone sits and eats together at langar, showing equality.

test.q: Who do Sikhs honor as the living Guru today?
test.why: Since 1708, Sikhs honor the scripture as the Guru.

test.q: A monk sweeps the ground ahead of her so she will not step on insects. Which tradition and idea?
test.why: Jain monks and nuns practice ahimsa toward even the smallest beings.

test.q: Which saying comes from the Analects?
choices: The highest excellence is like water.
All that we are is the result of what we have thought.
What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
There is one Creator; truth is the divine name.
test.why: Analects 15.23 teaches reciprocity; the others are Daoist, Buddhist and Sikh.

test.q: What did China's civil-service exams test?
test.why: The exams, from about 605 to 1905, were based on Confucian texts.

test.q: Which Daoist idea describes acting without forcing, like flowing water?
test.why: Wu wei is effortless action in harmony with nature.

test.q: What does a torii gate mark?
choices: the entrance to a Shinto shrine
the start of the Silk Road
test.why: The torii marks the passage into a Shinto shrine's sacred space.

test.q: Why do many people in Japan take part in both Shinto and Buddhist customs?
choices: Shinto and Buddhism are the same religion
the two traditions blended there over many centuries
test.why: Shinto and Buddhism blended in Japan for centuries, an example of syncretism.

write.prompt: How do these traditions teach people to treat others? Cite two or three texts from this unit, such as Analects 15.23, the Acaranga Sutra and the Bhagavad Gita. Explain what each tradition teaches and why, and compare them without judging.
tips: Name each text and its chapter or verse when you cite it.
Attribute every belief: 'Jains teach…', 'according to the Analects…'.
Compare what is alike and what is different; do not rank the traditions.
Use this unit's terms, such as ahimsa, ren and dharma, and explain each one.
